title: Weathering and Denudation
tagline: How rocks are broken down where they lie, and how the broken material is carried away

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The process names and landforms given here are the standard ones used in school geography; the boundary between weathering and denudation is a classroom convention rather than a law of nature, and is stated as such where it matters. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Define weathering and denudation and state clearly how the two differ.
Describe the physical, chemical and biological processes of weathering with examples.
Explain how chemical and biological weathering change the rock in a way that physical weathering does not.
Name the agents of denudation and the work each one does.
Relate the chief landforms of running water, wind, glaciers and waves to the process that produced them.

overview.intro: The surface of the Earth is constantly being worn down, and the work is done in two stages. In the first stage the rock is broken down where it lies, by the weather, by chemical action and by living things; this is weathering, and the broken material stays on the spot. In the second stage the loosened material is removed by running water, wind, glaciers, waves and gravity; this is denudation, and it is the removal of material rather than its breakdown. The two processes work together: weathering prepares the surface and denudation strips it. The landforms that ring every coast and cross every continent, from the V-shaped river valleys of the hills to the fjords of Norway and the dunes of the Sahara, are the result of these processes acting over thousands of years.

facts.label: Weathering
facts.value: Breakdown of rock in place, by physical, chemical or biological means

facts.label: Denudation
facts.value: Removal of weathered and loosened material by running water, wind, glaciers, waves and gravity

facts.label: Main agents
facts.value: Running water, wind, glaciers, waves and mass movement by gravity

facts.label: Result
facts.value: Landforms such as V-shaped valleys, meanders, dunes, U-shaped valleys and sea cliffs

learn.title: Weathering: the breakdown of rock in place

blocks.text: Weathering is the breakdown of rocks at or near the surface by physical, chemical and biological agencies, without any movement of the material. Physical or mechanical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces by such means as the freezing of water in cracks, the daily expansion and contraction of rock under heating and cooling, and the scraping action of wind, waves and glaciers. The other two agencies work on the rock in different ways: chemical weathering alters the minerals of the rock itself, and biological weathering is done by living things. All three leave the loosened material on the spot, and it is this material that denudation later carries away.

blocks.caption: Table: physical weathering
rows: Frost action
Water freezes in cracks, expands by about 9 per cent and prises the rock apart
Road stones cracking in a cold hill region
Thermal expansion
Repeated heating and cooling makes the outer surface expand and contract faster than the interior
Scaling of exposed rock in a desert
Abrasion
Rock fragments grind against each other, carried by wind, water or glaciers
Rounding of pebbles on a beach

items: Weathering breaks rock down; erosion and denudation carry the broken material away.
Physical weathering increases the surface area of the rock but does not change its chemical composition.
Physical weathering works best where there is a wide difference in temperature between day and night, or where water can freeze in the cracks.
Talus, or scree, is the accumulation of angular rock fragments at the foot of a cliff after frost action.
The broken fragments stay where they were broken, and they are the material on which the agents of denudation work.

blocks.text: Chemical weathering alters the minerals of the rock, so the composition of the rock is changed and not merely its size. Oxygen in the air and in water combines with minerals such as iron to form rust, which is called oxidation; water taken up by certain minerals, which swell and loosen the rock around them, is called hydration; and the most important process of all is carbonation, in which the carbon dioxide dissolved in rain forms a weak acid that dissolves limestone. Chemical weathering is fastest in warm, moist conditions. Biological weathering is done by living things: the roots of plants growing into cracks widen them and exert pressure, burrowing animals loosen the soil, lichens and mosses attack bare rock chemically and hold moisture against it, and the decay of organic matter gives out weak acids that work on the soil and on the rock beneath it.

blocks.caption: Table: chemical and biological weathering
rows: Oxidation
Oxygen in air and water combines with minerals such as iron to form rust and weaken the rock
Rusting of iron ore and brown staining of rocks
Carbonation
Carbon dioxide dissolved in rain forms a weak acid that dissolves limestone
Caves and swallow holes in limestone country
Root action
Roots widen existing cracks and exert pressure on the rock
A tree splitting a pavement slab
Lichens
Lichens on bare rock chemically attack the surface and hold moisture against it
Weathering of granite outcrops

items: Chemical weathering changes the composition of the rock and is fastest in warm, moist conditions.
Carbonation is the most widespread chemical process, because rainwater is always slightly acid and limestone is very soluble in it.
Biological weathering is slow in total but is very effective in loosening jointed rock.
The decay of organic matter is a biological process that both adds humus to the soil and gives out weak acids.
In nature the three agencies work together, so a weathered surface usually shows the marks of all of them.

blocks.text: Denudation is the wearing away of the land surface by the removal of the material that weathering has loosened. The chief agents are running water, wind, glaciers, waves and gravity. Running water does most of the work in humid regions: a river in its upper course cuts a steep V-shaped valley, in its middle course it meanders and floods, and in its lower course it deposits the load it has carried. Wind is the dominant agent in dry regions, where it deflates loose material and abrades the rock that stands in its way. Glaciers are powerful agents in cold regions, where they pluck and grind rock into U-shaped valleys. Waves cut cliffs, caves and stacks on exposed coasts, and gravity moves material down slopes directly as rockfalls and landslides.

blocks.caption: Table: agents of denudation and the landforms they produce
rows: Running water
Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution and deposition
V-shaped valleys, meanders, ox-bow lakes, alluvial fans, deltas, flood plains
Wind
Deflation, abrasion and deposition
Dunes, mushroom rocks, inselbergs, pedestals, wind shadows
Glaciers
Plucking, abrasion and deposition
U-shaped valleys, cirques, fjords, moraines, erratic boulders
Waves
Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution
Cliffs, caves, arches, stacks, stumps, wave-cut platforms
Gravity
Mass movement down slopes
Landslides, rockfalls, talus slopes, scree

items: Hydraulic action is the force of the water itself as a wave breaks and traps air in a crack.
Attrition is the grinding of rock fragments against one another during transport; abrasion is the scraping of rock by loaded fragments.
Corrasion is another name for abrasion, and solution is the chemical removal of soluble material such as limestone.
Deposition happens when a river loses energy, on entering a still water body or on reaching the sea, and builds a delta.
The same landform can be produced by more than one agent, so the evidence of the environment must be considered before deciding which agent was at work.

learn.title: Landforms, soil and the cycle of erosion

blocks.text: Weathering and denudation do not act steadily in one direction. Where the land is still being lifted, denudation cuts into it and the cycle is youthful, with steep V-shaped valleys and narrow divides. Where uplift has slowed, the valleys widen and the river meanders, and the cycle is mature, with broad valleys and gentle slopes. Where uplift has almost ceased, the rivers have cut down to a common base level and the cycle is old, with broad plains and low divides. Because the land is not always rising, these three stages often occur together in the same region, and it is their combination that gives a landscape its character.

items: Soil is formed from the accumulation of weathered rock material mixed with decayed organic matter, and it takes thousands of years to form a fertile layer.
Topsoil is the thin, dark, fertile upper layer rich in humus; subsoil lies beneath it and is poorer; bedrock is the unweathered rock at the base.
In a youthful stage the river has a steep gradient, a narrow channel and a V-shaped cross section.
In a mature stage the river has a gentle gradient and a meandering course, and it cuts through the flood plain instead of into it.
In an old stage the relief is low, the divides are worn down and the drainage is often confused and has lakes and marshes.

items.text: Explain why a river in its lower course builds a delta rather than a V-shaped valley.
items.note: In the upper course the river has a steep gradient, so it cuts downwards faster than it erodes sideways and the cross section is V-shaped. In the lower course the gradient is very gentle, so the current slows on reaching the sea, the carrying power falls and the load is deposited faster than it is removed. The deposition builds outwards from the mouth and a triangular delta is formed in still water.

items.text: How does a mushroom rock form, and what happens to it in the end?
items.note: A mushroom rock stands on a narrow pedestal because the rock at the base is softer and is attacked more vigorously by the wind, which scours it with sand and pebbles, while the harder cap above it is protected. The same wind that scours the base also undercuts it, so the pedestal grows thinner and thinner. One day the cap can no longer be supported and it falls, leaving a stump behind. The softer rock around it is then worn down to leave a low block on the surface, which is itself worn away, and the whole hill is finally levelled off.

figures.caption: Figure: Weathering and denudation compared
figures.description: Weathering breaks rock down where it lies and leaves the debris in place. Denudation removes that loosened material from the place where it was produced and carries it elsewhere.

figures.caption: Figure: Landforms of the three stages of the cycle of erosion
figures.description: In the youthful stage the river cuts a steep V-shaped valley; in the mature stage it meanders across a broad plain and leaves an ox-bow lake; in the old stage the relief is low and the divides are worn away.

keyPoints: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place; denudation is the removal of the loosened material.
Physical weathering includes frost action, thermal expansion and abrasion, and it does not change the chemical composition of the rock.
Chemical weathering includes oxidation, hydration and carbonation, and it is fastest in warm, moist conditions.
Biological weathering is caused by roots, burrowing animals, lichens and the decay of organic matter.
The agents of denudation are running water, wind, glaciers, waves and gravity.
Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution are the chief ways in which running water works.
Wind is the dominant agent of denudation in dry regions and works by deflation and abrasion.
Glaciers erode by plucking and abrasion and produce U-shaped valleys, cirques and fjords.
Running water produces V-shaped valleys, meanders, ox-bow lakes, alluvial fans and deltas.
The cycle of erosion passes through youthful, mature and old stages.
examFocus: Questions that ask for the difference between weathering and erosion expect the words 'in place' for weathering and 'removed and carried away' for erosion.
Frost action and carbonation are the two processes most often asked for by name, and both need a one-line explanation of the mechanism.
Landform questions are usually set as a match: V-shaped valley with running water, U-shaped valley with glaciers, mushroom rock with wind, stack with waves.
When explaining how a landform is formed, give the agent, the action and the result in that order; each of the three carries marks.
For a question on the cycle of erosion, state the stage, describe the drainage and the relief, and give one example of a landform of that stage.

vocabulary.meaning: The breakdown of rock at or near the surface without movement of the material.
The removal of weathered material from the land surface by natural agents.
The prising apart of rock by the expansion of water as it freezes in cracks.
The chemical weathering of limestone by weak carbonic acid in rain.
The removal and carrying away of loose material by wind.
The scraping of rock by rock fragments carried by wind, water or ice.
The quarrying of blocks of rock by a freezing glacier.
The sequence through which a landscape passes from youthful to mature to old as denudation works on it.

questions.prompt: The process by which rock is broken down at the surface without any movement of the material is called:
questions.explanation: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place. Erosion and denudation describe the removal and carrying away of the loosened material.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing erosion, which is the removal stage rather than the breakdown stage.

questions.prompt: The widening of cracks in limestone by slightly acidic rainwater is an example of:
questions.explanation: Rain absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and becomes a weak carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone and produces swallow holes, caves and caverns.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing oxidation, which applies to the rusting of iron-bearing minerals.

questions.prompt: U-shaped valleys are the characteristic landform of:
questions.explanation: A glacier plucks and abrades rock from the floor and the sides of its valley, widening and deepening it into a U shape. A river in its upper course cuts a narrow V-shaped valley.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing running water, which produces V-shaped valleys and meanders rather than U-shaped ones.

questions.prompt: Sea stacks and arches are formed by the action of:
questions.explanation: Waves erode the weaker rock of a headland by hydraulic action and abrasion, cutting caves that deepen into arches and finally leave isolated stacks and stumps.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing wind, which produces mushroom rocks and dunes rather than coastal stacks.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the removal of weathered material from the Earth's surface by running water, wind, glaciers, waves and gravity is called ________.
questions.explanation: Denudation is the removal stage of the process, while weathering is the breakdown stage that prepares the material for it.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'weathering', which describes the breakdown of the rock rather than its removal.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the removal of fine particles by wind is called ________, and the scraping of rock by wind-borne sand is called ________.
questions.explanation: Deflation is the lifting and carrying away of loose material, while abrasion is the mechanical wearing of rock by the sand that the wind carries.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the two terms, so that deflation is used for the scraping action.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between weathering and denudation, and state two agents of denudation.
questions.answer: Weathering is the breakdown of rocks at or near the surface by physical, chemical or biological means, and the broken material stays where it was produced. Denudation is the removal of that loosened material from the place of its origin and its transport to another place. The agents of denudation are running water, wind, glaciers, sea waves and gravity; two examples are running water, which cuts V-shaped valleys, and wind, which forms dunes.
questions.explanation: The distinction is between breaking down and carrying away, and the agents should be named with an example of the work each does.
questions.commonMistake: Describing denudation as another word for weathering, when the two are the two different halves of the same process.

questions.prompt: Explain how frost action breaks up rock, and name two conditions needed for it to be effective.
questions.answer: Frost action, also called freeze-thaw weathering, occurs when water enters cracks in the rock and freezes. Water expands by about 9 per cent of its volume as it turns to ice, and because the ice cannot escape from the crack it exerts pressure on the walls of the crack. Repeated cycles of freezing and thawing widen the crack until a block of rock is prised away. The two conditions are a supply of water that can enter the cracks, and temperatures that fall below freezing often enough, which is why the process is common in cold mountain regions.
questions.explanation: The mechanism, the effect of repeated cycles and the climatic conditions should all appear in the answer.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that water contracts when it freezes, which is the opposite of what happens.

questions.prompt: Explain how running water produces a meander and an ox-bow lake.
questions.answer: In the middle course of a river, where the gradient is gentle, the water strikes the outer bank of a bend with the greatest force, so that bank is undercut and eroded while the inner bank is built up by deposition. The bend therefore grows sharper and the river begins to swing in a loop called a meander. The neck of the meander becomes progressively narrower. Eventually the river cuts through the neck, leaving the former loop cut off from the river as an ox-bow lake, which later silts up and becomes a marsh.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that erosion on the outer bank and deposition on the inner bank make the bend grow until the neck is cut through.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the inner bank is eroded, which is exactly the opposite of what happens.

questions.prompt: Describe the work done by wind in a desert region, naming the two main processes and the landforms that each produces.
questions.answer: Wind does two main kinds of work in a desert. The first is deflation, in which the wind lifts and carries away fine loose material such as sand, silt and dust, leaving behind the coarse fragments that cannot be moved; this produces deflation hollows, and where a resistant rock mass is left standing alone it becomes an inselberg or a pedestal rock, and where a softer cap is left resting on a narrower stem a mushroom rock is formed. The second process is abrasion, in which the sand carried by the wind is thrown against the rock and files it away, deepening hollows and undercutting the softer rock at the base of a cliff, which produces the classic mushroom or pedestal shape and wind-blasted grooves. Where the wind drops its load, the material is deposited as sand dunes, which move in the direction of the prevailing wind, and as loess in sheltered areas beyond the dune belt.
questions.explanation: A full answer names the two processes, explains the mechanism of each and gives the landforms that follow from it.
questions.commonMistake: Naming only abrasion and omitting deflation, which is the process that actually removes and transports the material.

questions.prompt: Explain why the same landform may sometimes be attributed to different agents, and how the evidence of the surrounding environment helps to decide.
questions.answer: Different agents can produce shapes that look alike, because they all act by wearing rock away, so the shape alone is not enough to identify the agent. A flat-floored, steep-sided valley can be cut by a river, but it can also be carved by a glacier, and the two leave different marks. A rounded rock in a desert may be a wind pedestal, but it may equally be a boulder polished by glacier ice or by waves on a beach. The evidence of the environment has to be used instead. Climate gives the first clue: an arid climate, sparse vegetation and sand dunes point to wind; a cold climate with ice, snow and a history of glaciation points to a glacier; a humid climate with heavy rainfall and a river system points to running water; and a salty, wet coast with strong surf points to waves. Rock type gives the second: a glacier's U-shaped valley in a region of hard resistant rock is characteristic, while a soft rock with deep chemical weathering suggests that solution rather than mechanical action has been at work. The direction of the work gives the third: a V-shaped valley with a stream in its floor is fluvial, whereas a wide trough with striations and erratic boulders and a lake or fjord at its lower end is glacial. Only by combining climate, rock type and the marks left on the ground can the agent be identified with confidence.
questions.explanation: The reasoning is that shape is shared, so the decision must rest on environmental evidence, and the answer should show which evidence points to which agent.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one piece of evidence, for example climate, without showing how the rock type and the marks left on the ground confirm the decision.
